title: Given a tree and a non-empty list of employees/nodes (which may contain duplicates), return the deepest node whose subtree contains ALL of them. Deduplicate the targets, then in postorder count target nodes in each subtree (including the root), returning the deepest node containing every distinct target in O(N + K) time and O(N) space. Follow-up: if the tree is fixed but you receive thousands of queries, separate preprocessing cost from per-query cost using an Euler-tour and sparse table for O(1) LCA per pair.
shortTitle: Lowest Common Ancestor of N Nodes: deepest node whose subtree contains all targets
keyPoints: Deduplicate targets into a set before counting to prevent inflated required counts from duplicate entries
Post-order traversal counts how many distinct targets each subtree contains; the deepest node with a full count is the LCA
Single-query cost is O(N + K) time and O(N) space for the recursion and the target set
For many queries on a fixed tree, preprocess with an Euler tour and sparse table for O(1) pairwise LCA
Multi-target LCA folds pairwise: LCA(a, b, c) = LCA(LCA(a, b), c)
The counting approach is simpler and more general than trying to extend the two-node LCA algorithm directly

s1_definition.oneliner: Deduplicate the targets, count distinct targets per subtree in post-order, and return the deepest node whose subtree contains all of them.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **LCA of N nodes** – the deepest node whose subtree contains every target node in the given set.
- **Deduplication** – place targets in a `HashSet` so duplicates do not inflate the required count.
- **Post-order count** – each node returns how many distinct targets its subtree contains; the count is the sum of children's counts plus one if the node itself is a target.
- **Answer** – the deepest node whose count equals the number of distinct targets.
- **Follow-up** – for many queries on a fixed tree, preprocess with Euler tour and sparse table for O(1) pairwise LCA.
s1_definition.analogy: Compliance at the National Bank of India flags a group of employees in a suspicious transaction ring. HR needs the lowest-level manager who oversees every one of them. Starting from the bottom up, each manager counts how many of the flagged people fall under them. The deepest manager whose count reaches the full group size is the common boss of the entire ring.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Post-Order Counting

         CEO (count=3, all targets found → but not deepest)
        /    \
     VP1      VP2
    (2/2)    (1/2)
    /   \       \
  MGR1  MGR2   MGR3
  (1)   (1)    (1)

  Targets: {MGR1, MGR2}
  Post-order visits: MGR1(1), MGR2(1), VP1(2=full!) → VP1 is LCA
  CEO also has count=2, but VP1 was found first in post-order
```

```text
  Euler Tour (DFS order with depths)

  Visit:  CEO  VP1  MGR1  VP1  MGR2  VP1  CEO  VP2  MGR3  VP2  CEO
  Depth:   0    1    2     1    2     1    0    1    2     1    0

  LCA(MGR1, MGR2) = shallowest node between their first occurrences
  = VP1 (depth 1)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Lowest Common Ancestor of a set of nodes generalizes the classic two-node LCA. The clean approach is counting coverage: deduplicate the targets into a set, run a post-order traversal where each node reports how many distinct targets its subtree contains, and the deepest node with a full count is the answer. Post-order guarantees deepest-first discovery because children are visited before parents.

Deduplication is essential because duplicate targets from multiple reports would inflate the required count, making the LCA unfindable. The counting approach is simpler and more general than trying to extend the two-node algorithm with pairwise pairing.

The follow-up changes the economics entirely. If the tree is fixed but you receive thousands of queries, repeating a linear traversal each time is wasteful. Preprocessing with an Euler tour and sparse table gives O(1) pairwise LCA, and folding pairwise over K targets takes only K-1 constant-time pair queries. Recognizing this preprocessing-versus-per-query tradeoff is the senior-level insight the interviewer is testing.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, the fraud investigation team flags groups of employees and needs the lowest-level manager overseeing all of them. The org-tree service uses the counting traversal for one-off investigations and switches to the Euler-tour sparse table when a large case fires thousands of group queries against the same hierarchy.

Remember one sentence: deduplicate targets, count per subtree in post-order, and the deepest node with a full count is the LCA of the group.
